Apple_Alternaria Blotch.symptoms: Small dark brown to black leaf spots may enlarge, yellow surrounding tissue, and cause premature leaf drop.
Apple_Alternaria Blotch.possible_cause: Alternaria fungi may cause blotch symptoms, especially in warm, humid conditions; confirm locally because leaf-spot diseases overlap.
Apple_Alternaria Blotch.treatment: Remove fallen infected leaves, prune for airflow, and use only an apple-approved fungicide if local advice recommends it.
Apple_Alternaria Blotch.prevention: Keep the canopy open, remove diseased debris, avoid prolonged leaf wetness, and monitor during wet weather.

Apple_Apple Mosaic Virus.symptoms: Leaves may show pale yellow mottling, irregular mosaic patches or rings; vigor and fruit quality may decline.
Apple_Apple Mosaic Virus.possible_cause: Apple mosaic virus can spread through infected grafting or propagation material; symptoms vary by cultivar.
Apple_Apple Mosaic Virus.treatment: There is no curative treatment for infected trees; confirm diagnosis and consult local plant-health services about severely affected trees.
Apple_Apple Mosaic Virus.prevention: Use certified virus-free nursery and grafting material, clean tools, and never propagate from symptomatic trees.

Apple_Apple Scab.symptoms: Olive-green to dark velvety spots appear on leaves; fruit may develop rough, scabby or cracked lesions, and leaves may drop early.
Apple_Apple Scab.possible_cause: Venturia inaequalis survives in infected fallen leaves and spreads during wet spring weather.
Apple_Apple Scab.treatment: Remove infected fallen leaves and fruit; use an apple-labeled scab program only as recommended locally.
Apple_Apple Scab.prevention: Use resistant cultivars where suitable, manage leaf litter, prune for airflow, and follow local disease-risk guidance.

Apple_Black Rot.symptoms: On leaves, black rot can appear as small purple to brown spots that enlarge and may develop into circular lesions. Infected tissue can darken, and severe infections may contribute to leaf damage. Black rot can also affect fruit and woody tissues.
Apple_Black Rot.possible_cause: Black rot is caused by the fungus Diplodia seriata, formerly known as Botryosphaeria obtusa. The fungus can survive in dead wood, cankers, and mummified fruit and can enter through wounds.
Apple_Black Rot.treatment: Remove and properly dispose of mummified fruit, dead branches, twigs, and cankers that can act as sources of fungal inoculum. Prune affected woody tissue and use appropriate fungicides according to the product label and local recommendations.
Apple_Black Rot.prevention: Maintain good orchard sanitation, remove dead wood and mummified fruit, prune out cankers, reduce plant stress, and avoid conditions that allow prolonged moisture on plant tissues. Follow a locally recommended disease-management and fungicide program.

Apple_Brown Spot.symptoms: Brown or reddish spots may appear on leaves, sometimes with pale centers; severe cases can cause yellowing and early leaf drop.
Apple_Brown Spot.possible_cause: This label can refer to different fungal leaf-spot diseases; the precise pathogen varies by region and requires confirmation.
Apple_Brown Spot.treatment: Remove infected debris and reduce leaf wetness; seek local diagnosis before choosing a fungicide.
Apple_Brown Spot.prevention: Maintain orchard sanitation and airflow, avoid overhead irrigation when practical, and monitor during wet periods.

Apple_Cedar Apple Rust.symptoms: Bright yellow-orange spots appear on leaves; later, raised structures may form underneath and fruit can develop orange lesions.
Apple_Cedar Apple Rust.possible_cause: Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae requires apple and certain juniper or red cedar hosts to complete its life cycle.
Apple_Cedar Apple Rust.treatment: Established lesions cannot be cured; use preventive management only according to local extension recommendations and product labels.
Apple_Cedar Apple Rust.prevention: Choose resistant cultivars where available and manage nearby infected junipers where feasible and locally advised.

Apple_Grey Spot.symptoms: Small gray or tan spots with darker margins may develop, merge, and cause premature leaf drop.
Apple_Grey Spot.possible_cause: The name may describe different leaf-spot pathogens by region; confirm the cause before assigning a specific organism.
Apple_Grey Spot.treatment: Remove infected fallen leaves, improve airflow, and obtain local diagnosis before using fungicides.
Apple_Grey Spot.prevention: Remove diseased debris, reduce prolonged leaf wetness, and monitor new growth during wet weather.

Apple_Healthy.symptoms: No major visible disease symptoms detected.
Apple_Healthy.possible_cause: The leaf appears healthy based on the current AI prediction.
Apple_Healthy.prevention: Maintain proper watering, nutrition, sunlight, spacing, and regular monitoring.

Apple_Powdery Mildew.symptoms: White or gray powdery growth affects young leaves and shoots; leaves may curl, become narrow, and shoots may be stunted.
Apple_Powdery Mildew.possible_cause: Podosphaera leucotricha persists in infected buds and spreads in humid conditions.
Apple_Powdery Mildew.treatment: Prune out infected shoots where practical; use only an apple-labeled mildew treatment recommended locally.
Apple_Powdery Mildew.prevention: Use resistant cultivars where available, remove infected shoots, avoid excess nitrogen, and inspect young growth.

Cherry_Healthy.symptoms: No major visible disease symptoms detected.
Cherry_Healthy.possible_cause: The leaf appears healthy based on the current AI prediction.
Cherry_Healthy.prevention: Maintain proper watering, nutrition, sunlight, spacing, and regular monitoring.

Cherry_Powdery Mildew.symptoms: White powdery patches may appear on young leaves and shoots; leaves can curl or distort and shoot growth may be reduced.
Cherry_Powdery Mildew.possible_cause: Powdery mildew fungi, often Podosphaera species on cherry, are favored by humid air and dense growth.
Cherry_Powdery Mildew.treatment: Prune heavily affected shoots where practical; use a cherry-labeled product only if local guidance recommends it.
Cherry_Powdery Mildew.prevention: Maintain an open canopy, avoid excess nitrogen, remove infected shoots, and monitor young growth.

Grape_Black Measles.symptoms: Leaves may show interveinal yellowing or red discoloration with green veins and scorched margins; berries may develop dark spots or decay.
Grape_Black Measles.possible_cause: Grapevine measles is part of the esca trunk-disease complex associated with several wood-inhabiting fungi.
Grape_Black Measles.treatment: There is no reliably curative foliar spray; mark symptomatic vines and consult a viticulture specialist about trunk-disease management.
Grape_Black Measles.prevention: Use healthy planting material, protect pruning wounds according to local guidance, remove dead wood, and monitor vines.

Grape_Black Rot.symptoms: Grape leaves develop reddish-brown circular spots that enlarge as the disease progresses. Lesions may develop tan to brown centers with small black pycnidia in or around the center. Black rot can also cause dark, shriveled grape berries that become hard mummies.
Grape_Black Rot.possible_cause: Grape black rot is caused by the fungus Guignardia bidwellii. The pathogen can survive in mummified berries, old fruit clusters, and infected cane tissue, with spores spreading during wet spring conditions.
Grape_Black Rot.treatment: Remove and properly dispose of mummified berries, infected leaves, and diseased plant material. Use an appropriate fungicide program according to the product label and local agricultural recommendations, especially during periods when new infections are likely.
Grape_Black Rot.prevention: Maintain good vineyard sanitation by removing mummified fruit and infected plant material. Keep the canopy open to improve airflow and reduce prolonged leaf wetness, and follow a locally recommended fungicide management program.

Grape_Healthy.symptoms: No major visible disease symptoms detected.
Grape_Healthy.possible_cause: The leaf appears healthy based on the current AI prediction.
Grape_Healthy.prevention: Maintain proper watering, nutrition, sunlight, spacing, and regular monitoring.

Grape_Leaf Blight.symptoms: Brown or tan leaf lesions may expand and merge, causing leaf drying or early drop; patterns vary with the pathogen.
Grape_Leaf Blight.possible_cause: This broad class name can refer to different grape leaf-blight pathogens; it does not identify one organism conclusively.
Grape_Leaf Blight.treatment: Remove heavily infected debris, improve canopy airflow, and confirm the cause before selecting a grape-labeled product.
Grape_Leaf Blight.prevention: Maintain an open canopy, remove infected debris, reduce prolonged leaf wetness, and follow local vineyard guidance.

Grape_Powdery Mildew.symptoms: White-gray powdery patches appear on leaves, shoots, or berries; leaves may curl and infected berries can crack.
Grape_Powdery Mildew.possible_cause: Erysiphe necator causes grape powdery mildew and is favored by warm conditions and dense canopies.
Grape_Powdery Mildew.treatment: Use a grape-labeled mildew program only when recommended locally and follow the label; remove severely affected tissue where practical.
Grape_Powdery Mildew.prevention: Open the canopy, monitor early growth, use tolerant cultivars where suitable, and follow local mildew-risk advice.

Peach_Bacterial Leaf Spot.symptoms: Small water-soaked spots turn dark brown or purple and may drop out, creating a shot-hole appearance; severe cases cause defoliation.
Peach_Bacterial Leaf Spot.possible_cause: Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni is spread by rain splash, wet weather, and infected nursery material.
Peach_Bacterial Leaf Spot.treatment: There is no curative treatment for infected leaves; consult local orchard guidance before using any registered product because efficacy and crop safety vary.
Peach_Bacterial Leaf Spot.prevention: Plant clean stock, choose resistant cultivars where available, avoid overhead irrigation, and improve airflow.

Peach_Healthy.symptoms: No major visible disease symptoms detected.
Peach_Healthy.possible_cause: The leaf appears healthy based on the current AI prediction.
Peach_Healthy.prevention: Maintain proper watering, nutrition, sunlight, spacing, and regular monitoring.

Strawberry_Healthy.symptoms: No major visible disease symptoms detected.
Strawberry_Healthy.possible_cause: The leaf appears healthy based on the current AI prediction.
Strawberry_Healthy.prevention: Maintain proper watering, nutrition, sunlight, spacing, and regular monitoring.

Strawberry_Leaf Scorch.symptoms: Small dark purple or red spots enlarge into irregular brown areas; affected leaves look scorched, dry, and brittle.
Strawberry_Leaf Scorch.possible_cause: Diplocarpon earlianum commonly causes strawberry leaf scorch and can spread from infected leaves in splashing water.
Strawberry_Leaf Scorch.treatment: Remove heavily affected old leaves and improve airflow; use only a strawberry-labeled fungicide if locally recommended.
Strawberry_Leaf Scorch.prevention: Use healthy plants, remove infected debris, reduce leaf wetness, and maintain spacing and airflow.

Strawberry_Leaf Spot.symptoms: Small purple or reddish spots develop with pale tan or gray centers; severe infection can weaken leaves and reduce vigor.
Strawberry_Leaf Spot.possible_cause: Often associated with Mycosphaerella fragariae (Ramularia tulasnei), though other causes can resemble it.
Strawberry_Leaf Spot.treatment: Remove badly affected leaves, reduce leaf wetness, and use only registered strawberry treatments after confirming the disease.
Strawberry_Leaf Spot.prevention: Plant disease-free stock, use resistant cultivars where available, remove debris, and avoid overhead irrigation where practical.

Strawberry_Powdery Mildew.symptoms: White powdery growth may appear under leaves; leaf margins can curl upward and become reddish or purplish, and flowers or fruit may be affected.
Strawberry_Powdery Mildew.possible_cause: Podosphaera aphanis is favored by moderate temperatures, humid air, and dense growth.
Strawberry_Powdery Mildew.treatment: Remove severely affected tissue where practical and use a strawberry-labeled treatment only if local guidance recommends it.
Strawberry_Powdery Mildew.prevention: Use tolerant cultivars where available, maintain airflow, avoid excess nitrogen, and inspect leaf undersides.

Tomato_Alfalfa Mosaic Virus.symptoms: Leaves may show yellow mottling, mosaic patterns, rings, or necrotic streaks; plants may be stunted and fruit quality may decline.
Tomato_Alfalfa Mosaic Virus.possible_cause: Alfalfa mosaic virus can be transmitted by aphids and may persist in infected host plants or plant material.
Tomato_Alfalfa Mosaic Virus.treatment: There is no curative treatment; remove confirmed infected plants where practical and manage host weeds according to local guidance.
Tomato_Alfalfa Mosaic Virus.prevention: Use healthy transplants, manage weed hosts and aphids, clean tools, and monitor plants regularly.

Tomato_Bacterial Leaf Spot.symptoms: Small water-soaked spots turn dark brown or black, often with yellow halos; leaves may drop and fruit may develop raised scabby lesions.
Tomato_Bacterial Leaf Spot.possible_cause: Xanthomonas bacteria can spread through infected seed or transplants, splashing water, and handling wet plants.
Tomato_Bacterial Leaf Spot.treatment: Remove severely affected material where practical, avoid wet foliage handling, and seek local advice on registered products; copper may only suppress disease partially.
Tomato_Bacterial Leaf Spot.prevention: Use tested seed and clean transplants, rotate away from tomato and pepper, sanitize tools, avoid overhead irrigation, and manage debris.

Tomato_Early Blight.symptoms: Dark brown circular spots with concentric rings may appear on older leaves. Leaves can yellow and drop as the disease progresses.
Tomato_Early Blight.possible_cause: Early blight is commonly associated with the fungus Alternaria solani and is favored by warm, humid conditions.
Tomato_Early Blight.treatment: Remove severely affected leaves, improve air circulation, avoid overhead watering, and use an appropriate fungicide according to the product label.
Tomato_Early Blight.prevention: Use healthy planting material, avoid prolonged leaf wetness, remove infected plant debris, and practice crop rotation.

Tomato_Healthy.symptoms: No major visible disease symptoms detected in the uploaded image.
Tomato_Healthy.possible_cause: The leaf appears healthy based on the current AI prediction.
Tomato_Healthy.treatment: No disease treatment is indicated. Continue normal crop care and monitor the plant regularly.
Tomato_Healthy.prevention: Maintain proper watering, nutrition, sunlight, spacing, and regular inspection for early signs of disease.

Tomato_Late Blight.symptoms: Large irregular water-soaked green-gray lesions turn dark and spread rapidly; pale growth may appear at edges in humid weather, and stems or fruit may be affected.
Tomato_Late Blight.possible_cause: Phytophthora infestans spreads rapidly in cool, wet conditions from infected plants or volunteer hosts.
Tomato_Late Blight.treatment: Act quickly and contact local extension services; use only registered late-blight products according to local alerts and labels.
Tomato_Late Blight.prevention: Use healthy transplants, manage volunteer tomatoes and potatoes, reduce leaf wetness, improve airflow, and monitor regional alerts.

Tomato_Leaf Mold.symptoms: Pale green or yellow patches form on upper leaf surfaces, with olive-gray fuzzy growth underneath; leaves may brown and die.
Tomato_Leaf Mold.possible_cause: Passalora fulva (formerly Cladosporium fulvum) is favored by high humidity and poor airflow, especially in greenhouses.
Tomato_Leaf Mold.treatment: Remove heavily infected leaves, improve ventilation, reduce humidity, and use only a locally recommended tomato-labeled product if needed.
Tomato_Leaf Mold.prevention: Ventilate protected crops, avoid crowding, water at soil level, remove crop debris, and use resistant cultivars where suitable.

Tomato_Leaf Mosaic Virus.symptoms: Leaves may show light and dark green mosaic, puckering, narrowing, or distortion; plants may be stunted and fruit quality may decline.
Tomato_Leaf Mosaic Virus.possible_cause: The label may refer to Tomato mosaic virus or a related virus spread by infected seed, transplants, hands, tools, or debris.
Tomato_Leaf Mosaic Virus.treatment: There is no curative treatment; remove confirmed infected plants where practical and seek diagnosis if the virus identity affects management.
Tomato_Leaf Mosaic Virus.prevention: Use certified virus-free seed and transplants, clean hands and tools, remove infected debris, and manage weed hosts.

Tomato_Powdery Mildew.symptoms: Pale yellow patches and sometimes white powdery growth develop on leaves; leaves can dry and drop as disease progresses.
Tomato_Powdery Mildew.possible_cause: Powdery mildew fungi such as Oidium neolycopersici or Leveillula taurica may be involved, depending on region.
Tomato_Powdery Mildew.treatment: Remove heavily affected leaves where practical, improve airflow, and use only a tomato-labeled treatment recommended locally.
Tomato_Powdery Mildew.prevention: Maintain spacing and airflow, avoid excess nitrogen, inspect foliage regularly, and use resistant varieties where available.

Tomato_Septoria Leaf Blotch.symptoms: Many small circular spots with gray or tan centers and dark margins appear on lower leaves; tiny black fruiting bodies may be visible, followed by yellowing and leaf drop.
Tomato_Septoria Leaf Blotch.possible_cause: Septoria lycopersici survives on infected debris and spreads by splashing water.
Tomato_Septoria Leaf Blotch.treatment: Remove infected lower leaves, dispose of diseased debris, water at soil level, and use only locally recommended tomato-labeled fungicides if needed.
Tomato_Septoria Leaf Blotch.prevention: Rotate crops, remove volunteer tomatoes and debris, stake plants for airflow, mulch to reduce soil splash, and avoid overhead watering.

Tomato_Target Spot.symptoms: Brown circular lesions with concentric rings develop on leaves and may also affect stems or fruit; severe infection can cause defoliation.
Tomato_Target Spot.possible_cause: Corynespora cassiicola is favored by warm, humid conditions and prolonged leaf wetness.
Tomato_Target Spot.treatment: Remove heavily infected leaves, improve airflow, and use a registered tomato fungicide only if local guidance recommends it.
Tomato_Target Spot.prevention: Use healthy transplants, rotate crops, remove infected residue, maintain spacing, and monitor in humid weather.

Tomato_Tomato Leaf Curl Virus.symptoms: Leaves curl upward or inward, become small or yellow, and plants may be stunted with reduced flowering and fruit set.
Tomato_Tomato Leaf Curl Virus.possible_cause: Tomato leaf-curl viruses are commonly transmitted by whiteflies; the specific virus depends on the region.
Tomato_Tomato Leaf Curl Virus.treatment: There is no curative treatment; remove confirmed infected plants where recommended and manage whiteflies with locally approved integrated pest management.
Tomato_Tomato Leaf Curl Virus.prevention: Use resistant varieties where available, protect young plants from whiteflies, remove infected plants and weed hosts, and use insect exclusion where suitable.

Tomato_Verticillium Wilt.symptoms: Lower leaves yellow in V-shaped patterns or develop dead margins; plants may wilt during warm periods and show vascular discoloration.
Tomato_Verticillium Wilt.possible_cause: Soilborne Verticillium dahliae or V. albo-atrum can infect roots and persist in soil.
Tomato_Verticillium Wilt.treatment: There is no reliable curative treatment for infected plants; confirm the diagnosis and consult local guidance on resistant varieties and rotation.
Tomato_Verticillium Wilt.prevention: Plant resistant varieties, avoid moving infested soil, manage weed hosts, and rotate with non-host crops where locally effective.
